ARC: The Seventh Invasion (643–645)

=== EPISODE 31: Four Dragons (643)
The Second Emperor of the West resides in the Palace. Seventeen years ago he murdered his brothers to become the Son of Heaven, and he has spent every year since folding nations under imperial rule — the Turks, the Xueyantuo, the Tibetans.
The inner palace is a country of its own — so many women the hall cannot hold them all at once, silk stacked like tribute, a very large harem that moves when he moves.
He’s known by many names. The Heaven-Sent General. The Khan of Heaven.
One more thing about him, which nobody in Samhan quite believes when they are told it: nobody says his name.
He never quite forbids it. The two characters of his given name simply vanish from the empire, quietly: a ministry renamed because one of them sat in its title, a bodhisattva’s name shortened by a syllable, scribes copying old books leaving one stroke off — and everyone understands.
herald: …They don’t say his name? At all?
herald: They don’t write it either. Not on paper.
So the Second Emperor of the West is a man who has not heard another person say his own name since he was crowned, and there is nobody left alive who is allowed to.
The Grand Minister is dying. At the foot of the bed the court diarist, Chu Suiliang, writes down everything the emperor says.
weizheng: Your Majesty. When I am gone, there will be no one left to tell you no.
taizong: Why else do you think I put up with you for twenty years.
taizong: With bronze for a mirror, a man straightens his robes. / With history for a mirror, he sees the rise and fall of states. / With a man for a mirror, he sees his own faults. / …Today I lose one of my mirrors.
taizong: The Great Tang is still a young dynasty. / We must not repeat the mistakes of the Sui…! / Not if the western dream is to be realised.
chusuiliang: The western dream?
taizong: The great revival of the Central Plain dynasties. / Han was the finest civilisation in the world. / And then— / Four hundred years. Four hundred years of being savaged by barbarians!! / Sui reunified it, then fell in less than thirty years because of that lunatic Emperor Yang. / And here I am. The Prince of Qin!
By the next spring the dream has left the sickroom. Over every ward gate in Chang’an the sign-painters letter it in gold on red, THE GREAT TANG DREAM, each banner at the same height and the same distance from the next. Nobody can say who ordered it, which is how the best orders travel.
Later that month Chu Suiliang brings in the reports from everywhere the empire touches.
chusuiliang: From India — they say the monk Xuanzang is still on his pilgrimage! / Though he sends back the strangest tales — flying monkeys and the like, / and in the western regions a new empire… Islam? A new teaching they follow. / Persia and Rome are said to have fallen, so it must be a formidable power. / And in the east — the King of Goryeo has been murdered by his own subject…
taizong: Wait. / Gai Suwen…?
Chang’an writes the name without the Yeon. Yeon, 淵, was the given name of the emperor’s late father, and nobody in this palace writes it. It is an old house. Nearly seven hundred years ago, in Jolbon, its crow-clan chieftain Yeon Tabal looked down at a soaked exile called Jumong and weighed him.
taizong: The King of Goryeo was a friend I valued. / His name… ah… / …Yeongnyu! King Yeongnyu!
Everything is in place. It has been for some time; he was simply waiting to be bored enough.
chusuiliang: Majesty, we have invaded six times already — and you would go again?
taizong: Because I have not gone myself. / Life is not theory. It is practice.
He launches the Seventh Invasion of Goguryeo. It’s the seventh army out of the West, and the first he leads himself. The clerks need three days to read the muster aloud. Horse from the frontier. Foot from the rivers. Five hundred hulls riding low with a year of grain.
Four dragon banners go up over the muster: white, red, blue and black.
The fifth banner has no name on it at all. Everyone knows whose it is.
Two of the four dragons were born on the steppe. The Red Dragon is a steppe prince who keeps felt tents inside the capital walls. The White Dragon walked his whole tribe across the border as a boy. The steppe has its own title for the emperor, and he answers to it. Even his favourite horses came from out there. The Black Dragon is the empress’s brother. He argued against this war in council. He’s riding to it anyway.
## The Third Leg
In the third month an envoy arrives from Pyongyang with a request nobody in the Ministry of Rites has seen before. The new master of Goguryeo would like some Daoists.
Goguryeo envoy: The Mangniji says a cauldron stands on three legs. / We have the Buddha. We have Confucius. / He would like the third leg, if the Son of Heaven can spare one.
taizong: He wants Laozi? / Give him Laozi. Our house descends from the old man anyway. Let Goguryeo bow to my ancestor and call it theology.
Eight Daoists go east with a copy of the Daodejing. In Pyongyang the Mangniji gives them lodgings, and the lodgings he gives them are temples. The monks are moved out the same week, with their bells.
A young monk named Shinsung carries the smallest bell down the hill himself, to a lesser house that has no frame to hang it from, and sets it on the floor. He does not complain to anyone. The bell stays on the floor for twenty-five years.
## Three Choices
In the ninth month an envoy comes from Silla, which is losing fortresses to Baekje faster than it can count them, and asks for an army. The Second Emperor offers him a choice of three.
taizong: One. I send the Khitan and the Mohe into Liaodong, and Goguryeo looks north for a year. / Two. I give you a few thousand red coats and Tang banners. Stand them on your walls. Baekje will think I have come, and run. / Three.
taizong: Your country is ruled by a woman, and your neighbours despise you for it. That is why they keep coming. / I could send you one of my own clan to be your king, with a few soldiers to look after him. When the country is safe, you may have it back.
The envoy says yes, and then no, and then nothing at all. The emperor watches him for a while.
taizong: A mediocre man. Not the sort a country sends when it is drowning.
The report reaches Surabol in the twelfth month. The Harmony Council has the third option read aloud twice. Bidam reads it once, and folds it small.
bidam: He offers us a king the way a temple puts out rice for a stray. / …And there are men in this hall who would bow for the bowl.
## Longmen Field
In a poor field at Longmen, a farmer named Xue Rengui is planning to rebury his ancestors. Millet, rammed earth, a hut that doesn’t pretend to be anything. He has the right soil for graves. He doesn’t yet know he has the wrong year for quiet.
The cloth on his back is plain yellow peasant hemp. Not a banner. Not the white armour the mountain will learn later. Just the cheapest dye the village still sells, the colour of millet at the wrong hour. He hoes. His wife, Liu, keeps the hut door.
The Son of Heaven is calling up troops for Liaodong. The edict reaches villages that have never seen a palace, and wives who have never left the furrow.
The edict comes on red paper, pasted to the well-house wall at the height of a man’s eyes: SERVE THE EMPEROR. Under it, in smaller characters, the quota. It does not ask for Xue Li. It asks for one man from every household with the right number of hands, and any man with hands will do.
xuerengui: The mounds… they’re not done. / Not the dirt. The hands. / The edict — I heard it. I did.
xueliu: Mounds don’t wait because a man is short of hands. / And the edict doesn’t wait either. / You’re not a hoe. You’re a ji. As far as I can tell.
xuerengui: The ji is in the shed. / The yellow clothes are here. / Liu. If I go — this door.
xueliu: I’ll shut the door. / Don’t you start worrying about doors. / Talent needs its hour. If this is the hour — then go.
The chronicler does not invent her sentence. The Xin Tangshu already wrote it down, and it is sharper than anything a field would volunteer twice.
[QUOTE Xin Tangshu (新唐書) bk. 111, biography of Xue Rengui (薛仁貴) — speech of his wife, née Liu (妻柳)] A man of talent that outstrips his age must meet his hour before it can issue. Now the Son of Heaven himself campaigns against Liaodong and seeks fierce generals: this is a time rarely met. Why should you not seek merit and make yourself known? When you return in wealth and honour, it will not be too late to bury them.
He goes. She is right, and a man who can lift a ji should not spend the invasion stacking earth for the dead.
xuerengui: …Ancestors. Wait a little longer. / Until I come back carrying this ji. / The yellow clothes — I’ll leave them here.
He presents himself to general Zhang Shigui and signs his name under the Tang muster. The clerk writes Xue Rengui. The clerk does not look up. History will.
[QUOTE Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 83, biography of Xue Rengui] Xue Rengui was a man of Longmen in Jiangzhou. At the end of Zhenguan, Taizong campaigned in person against Liaodong; Rengui presented himself to General Zhang Shigui, answered the muster, and asked to go.
His weapon is the same one the storytellers later give to Lü Bu: the fangtian ji — crescent blade and spear-point on one shaft. In the Longmen shed it is a farmer’s choice. In the chronicle it becomes the shape you see before you see his face.
Later opera won’t leave Liu in the hut. It puts her in a cold kiln and gives her a fuller name the histories never wrote. And a song. Lovely song. Not history.
[QUOTE Jingju Fenhewan (京劇《汾河灣》, also 仁貴打雁) — opening of Liu Yingchun; theatrical/folk, not the Tang official histories] My husband enlisted; there is no word. Mother and child suffer in a cold kiln.
By summer the yellow hemp is on a peg in Longmen, and the man who wore it is at Stallion Mountain, under the same Emperor who called him out of the field.
Yodong has never opened its gates to the West. Not for the Sui. Not in three summers. Here come the dragons…!

=== EPISODE 32: Yodong (645)
Goguryeo has spent fourteen years building a wall of forts along the river. The Blue Dragon simply walks around it. He shows his banners on the middle road, then turns north in the night. By morning his horse are across an unwatched ford. The first fortress shuts its gates. It holds exactly as long as the gates do.
The New Fortress doesn’t fall. The emperor’s cousin spends ten days under its walls and leaves with nothing. So the Blue Dragon posts a guard on it and turns south. The next fort lasts a little over ten days. Seven hundred men Yeon sent to hold it are taken in the gate. They ask to serve the emperor instead.
taizong: Their homes are all in Gasi, I am told. / If they fight for Us, the Mangniji will kill every wife and child they have. / To gain one man’s arm by wiping out his house — that We cannot bring Ourselves to do. Send them home.
They go home with grain for the road. It is a kindness, and it is also arithmetic: seven hundred men who have seen the size of this army will describe it to Gasi better than any envoy could.
Between the army and the walls lies the Liao marsh. Two hundred li of mud. A Sui host once went in up to the knee and came out as a song. The emperor’s engineer lays a road of earth across it, wide enough for carts. When the last wagon is over, the emperor has the road torn up. Nobody goes home the way they came. He wants every man in the column to know it.
Then the Eastern Fortress itself. It held off the last dynasty for three summers and never opened. The Blue Dragon has already driven one sortie back through the gate when the emperor arrives. He rides to the moat with a sack of earth across his saddle and throws it in. His officers can’t be seen carrying less than him. They carry two. The army rings the walls a hundred deep and beats the drums until the ground answers.
Inside the walls there is a shrine to Jumong, the Holy King who founded the country. A coat of chain mail hangs in it, and a long sharp spear, and the town will tell you both came down from heaven in the days of the old Yan. By the eighth day stones are coming over the parapet. The elders choose a girl from the town, wash her, paint her, dress her in red silk and a bride’s crown, and walk her up to the shrine to be given to the god.
👰: It’s… heavy. The dress. / …Tell my mum. Tell her I didn’t cry.
🔔: The Holy King… is smiling. / He has taken his bride! This city will stand whole!
They close the shrine door on her. The record does not say whether anyone opens it again.
[QUOTE Zizhi Tongjian (資治通鑑) bk. 197] In the city was a shrine to Jumong, and in the shrine a coat of chain mail and a sharp spear, which they falsely said had come down from heaven in the age of the Former Yan. When the siege grew desperate they adorned a beautiful woman as a wife for the god, and the shamans said: Jumong is pleased; the city will surely stand whole.
The Holy King isn’t consulted again. The Blue Dragon’s throwers hurl rocks the size of grain jars over the walls. Towers roll up to the parapet. On the twelfth day a south wind rises. They fire the south-west tower, and the wind carries it into town. When the gate gives, the clerks count ten thousand dead, then lose interest and count the grain. The fortress a million men couldn’t open has lasted twelve days.
Veterans spit and say the real argument is still ahead: not this eastern gate, but Ansi, where stone has already outlasted more emperors than the court will admit over wine.
Then the Second Emperor rides on to look at Ansi, and the man who holds it comes out onto the wall to look back. Nobody on the Tang side ever writes down his name.
yangmanchun: You will simply… / go down in history as a butcher without mercy…! / People with souls will never worship you…!
taizong: History? I am the one writing it. / You will vanish, a nameless barbarian, / and I will remain the greatest emperor history has known. / To light up the civilised — and the savage— / that is my power.
yangmanchun: Civilised? You call this civilisation…? / You trample them, you kill them, and then you stand on the pile and call it civilisation.
## The Rest of the Line
Meanwhile the rest of the line comes down like roof tiles. The clerks file it in a single column. At one fort Yeon’s riders break out and put a spear into the White Dragon’s waist. He has it bound and is back in the saddle by evening. The fort’s lord opens the gate anyway. Out on the southern cape, the fleet takes another in a month. Of all the forts Yeon spent fourteen years hauling stone for, two still fly Goguryeo’s banners.
Goguryeo has been here before. To learn what one bad afternoon can cost a king, we go back four hundred years…!

=== EPISODE 33: Boiling River (244) [flashback]
King Dongchun picks a fight over a diplomatic spat. The war that comes back at him starts on a river named for boiling.
The spat is this: Goguryeo raided the western commandery, the empire sent a general called Guanqiu Jian to explain why that was a mistake, and Goguryeo met him at the Boiling River and won, and then won again.
So the king took five thousand horse out to win a third time, on ground he had not looked at, and lost eighteen thousand men in an afternoon.
dongchun: …I did not look at the ground.
Hwando is burned. The king runs east with a handful of men and is saved by a single officer who dresses in the royal robes and walks out to be killed in his place.
Goguryeo takes forty years to be a kingdom again. It is the first time in this story that a Samhan capital burns because of one bad afternoon, and it is not the last, and every king in this record has heard about it.
Four hundred years later, another Goguryeo army marches to meet an emperor in the open. In the Tang line, a farmer puts on white…!

=== EPISODE 34: Stallion Mountain (645)
By summer the farmer from Longmen is no longer a name on a muster roll. He is at Stallion Mountain, under the same Emperor who called him out of the yellow hemp.
At Stallion Mountain the Second Emperor does not wait behind the line.
taizong: I myself am the vanguard…!
Goguryeo sends a relief army — Go Yeonsu and Go Hyejin, tens of thousands under banners that think numbers are an argument.
In the Tang line stands a guard captain whose accent still has the sea in it. Sul Gedu left Silla twenty-four winters ago, in the hold of a merchant ship. When the emperor called for volunteers, he put his own name down. It’s the only way a foreigner gets a captain’s sash. Across the field, the enemy’s banners are close enough to read.
🪖: Hey, Captain Xue. That lot over there… they say they’re Samhan men. / Aren’t you from Samhan as well?
xuejitou: Samhan. Silla. / In Silla they count your bones before they hire you. Doesn’t matter how big your talent is or how big your deeds — wrong bones, and you don’t get over the wall. You just don’t. / So I crossed the sea. To walk in and out at the Son of Heaven’s side with a cap and a sash and a sword. / …That’ll do me.
The soldier laughs, not sure he was meant to. Sul Gedu ties off his helmet cord and does not look at the banners again.
In the Tang line a low officer decides the field needs a mark it cannot look away from. He puts on white armour — not for mourning, for visibility — hangs two bows at his waist, takes up the fangtian ji, and rides into the front so hard the relief army has to notice him or die without knowing why.
xuerengui: Make a path. / If you will not — the ji will.
No one in the Goguryeo line stops him for long, and the Tang officers, seeing the white coat cut a road, pour in after it. The formation breaks. The mountain learns a new colour.
taizong: Who is that man in white armour. / The one at the tip of the spear.
lishiji: Xue Rengui, Your Majesty. / A soldier… who was a farmer.
They bring him up. Dirt on the white. Blood on the crescent of the ji. He kneels like a man who has never been in a palace and does not intend to apologise for it.
taizong: My old generals are all aged. / I have been looking for a fierce one to entrust the frontier to — and I find none better than you. / I am less happy about gaining Liaodong than about gaining you.
xuerengui: A farmer… how could he dare. / This ji only widened Your Majesty’s road a little.
They give him gold, silk, a general’s title, and a place among the men who stand at the northern gate. The white coat stays. So does the ji.
When the dust settles, the two relief commanders walk into the Tang camp and surrender. Thirty-six thousand men walk in behind them. The officers are sent inland, to be subjects far from any border. The common soldiers are sent home. The three thousand Mohe riders who came south with them are marched into a valley and buried alive.
Go Yeonsu does not live out the year. The records say he died of grief, which is the only cause of death the Tang ever let a surrendered general keep.
There is another foreigner in the reckoning that night. Riding over the ground where the Goguryeo centre stood, the emperor finds Sul Gedu farther in than any of his own men got, face down among the dead he made.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 47, Biographies 7, Seol Gyedu] Reaching Liaodong, he fought the men of Goguryeo below Stallion Mountain; he went deep, fought hard and died, and his merit was ranked first. The emperor asked what manner of man he was, and those about him reported that he was Xue Jitou, a man of Silla. The emperor wept and said: “Our own men still fear death and look about them and will not advance, yet a man of a foreign country has died in Our cause. How shall We repay his merit?” He asked the man’s companions and learned the wish of his life; he took off the imperial robe and covered him with it, granted him the office of Grand General, and buried him with full rites.
The cap, the sash and the sword, more or less. He gets them lying down.
Fame is a short leash. Before the army even settles into the Ansi siege, Goguryeo stops trying to kill the man in white in the open and starts trying to keep him.
They take him in a night fight east of the Liao — nets, numbers, the ji knocked from his hands — and drag him inland to a lesser fortress that is not Ansi and does not want to be famous. Iron on the wrists. A cell under the wall. The white coat cut off him like a trophy.
xuerengui: …The ji. / Where is the ji.
They laugh. A farmer asking for his farming tool.
Then a runner comes up the stair, out of breath.
goguard_a: The Second Emperor… is coming this way. / Tonight. To this fortress. Holy King, look down.
Xue Rengui hears it the way a chained animal hears the key.
xuerengui: …Before His Majesty arrives. / I will have to be out.
He breaks the irons. He breaks the door. The white coat only made him easy to see.
He finds the ji on a rack in the yard, still sticky from someone else’s hands, and takes the wall the way water takes a crack. By the time the Second Emperor’s banners show on the ridge, the cell is empty and the fortress is explaining itself to no one.
taizong: …That white coat again. / Arriving before Us, I see.
xuerengui: I could not keep Your Majesty waiting. / The chains… were impolite.
The Second Emperor laughs once — short, relieved — and does not ask how. A sovereign who has to ask how has already lost the man.
Among the prisoners taken at the mountain are two boys, eleven and eight, sent south with the baggage train by a father who thought the rear was safer.
taizong: So. Gai Suwen’s sons. / Your father killed his king. I killed my brothers. / So you see, he and I understand one another.
taizong: Here is my offer. / Kneel, call yourselves servants of the Great Tang, and I will give you both titles. / A house in Chang’an, silk, a name. Things Goryeo will never give you.
namgun: Brother.
Namseng is eleven. He works out, quite quickly, that the Second Emperor wants two and will settle for one, and that only one of them has to be the one who refuses.
namseng: Your Majesty. My brother is small. He understands nothing. / It is I who refuse. Give the punishment to me.
taizong: …You are the elder?
namseng: I am.
They flog him in front of his brother and send them both back across the Liao in the spring, as a gesture. Namgun does not speak for the whole journey.
namgun: You took it for me.
namseng: I am the elder.
The Second Emperor isn't the first emperor to come for Goguryeo. The last one met a general who surrendered seven times…!

=== EPISODE 35: Colossal River (612) [flashback]
Emperor Yang of Sui invades Goguryeo in the year 612.
On the Colossal River, Ulchi Munduk breaks the Western Army. A century later, men will still point at other rivers and hope for the same appetite.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 44, Biographies — Ulchi Munduk; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2, p. 412 · cf. Suishu (隋書) bk. 81, Account of Goguryeo] Your divine strategy has fathomed the heavens; your subtle reckoning has exhausted the earth. Your merit in victory is already high — know sufficiency, and I pray you stop.
Munduk walks into the enemy camp himself first, to look at them. He surrenders seven times on the way south and runs seven times, and each running pulls the Western army further from its supply and closer to a river.
Munduk is honored with the title “The Defender” after the battle.
Yodong fell. The forts fell. One wall is left, held by a madman whose name nobody wrote down…!

=== EPISODE 36: Ansi (645)
The Guardian of Ansi Fortress is an eccentric man. When Yeon took the country, the Guardian refused him to his face. He kept the old king’s colours on the wall. Yeon had drowned a whole court for less. He looked at that wall, weighed the siege, and rode away. Ansi answers to no one.
Nobody writes his name down. To the people inside the walls he is just the chief, and that turns out to be enough.
Tang supply clerk: They will not give us his name. Only the Wall that Stopped an Emperor — as if a wall could have a pulse.
Another clerk: And they say the Eternal General is standing behind him. / Just put it down in the books as “unfinished.”
[FLASHBACK 642 Yeon at Ansi]
  gesomun: Ansi… so that man is still alive. / He dares refuse the Supreme Commander’s order?
  yangmanchun: I have heard that a true man needs only / one person to cherish, / and one person to serve, / and that is enough.
The ring at his hip is Goguryeo iron — a hollow circle the same red as the wall.
Six hundred li to the south, a Silla marshal had said something close to the same thing, to a queen, on the day she was crowned. Neither man will ever learn of the other.
The Second Emperor tries the wall first. When the wall does not work he tries the ground, which is the sort of thing only an empire can afford to try. Red wings on the parapet watch him do it.
Tang hauler: How many baskets is that now?
Another hauler: Don’t count. It gets heavier when you count.
Ansi soldier: Chief, that’s sixty days they’ve been at it.
yangmanchun: Then it’s sixty nights for us. Pass the stone.
Five hundred thousand man-days, sixty days of hauling, and a mountain of packed earth rises outside the south wall until its crown looks down into the fortress. From up there you can count the cook fires.
Then it rains, and the mountain slumps — sideways, into the wall it was built to overlook, taking a stretch of Ansi down with it. Both sides stare at the gap.
Ansi soldier: Chief, the wall—
yangmanchun: Never mind the wall. Who’s up on that thing right now?
The officer who was supposed to be holding the mound has stepped away.
Ansi soldier: …There’s nobody up there.
yangmanchun: Then it’s ours.
A few hundred men come out through the gap, take the mountain, pile timber on its slope and set it alight. The Tang cannot get near it for three days.
The Second Emperor has Fu Fuai, the officer who left the mound, beheaded, and orders three days of assault.
On the second day an arrow finds the helmet. Whether it was the wall or a stone the size of a cooking-pot, the lacquered bowl leaves his head and rings once on packed earth, then keeps rolling. Sweat. Yellow camp light. For the first time the face is simply there.
Then the cold comes early, the grass on the plain gives out, and there is nothing to feed the horses.
That day, for the first time in his life, the Second Emperor knew defeat and retreat.
[QUOTE Zizhi Tongjian (資治通鑑) Tang Zhenguan 19 (645), return from Liaodong; Zhonghua Shuju ed., vol. 13 · cf. Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 199上, Eastern Barbarians — Goguryeo] Had [the Grand Minister] been alive, he would not have let me make this expedition.
taizong: With all the armies under heaven, how was I humiliated by so small a barbarian land?
After the battle, the Guardian of Ansi is added to the Great Heroes of Goguryeo.
gesomun: Madman… / Still — he does what must be done.
On the day the army turned for home, the Second Emperor sent a hundred bolts of silk up to the wall, for a man whose name he never learned.
yangmanchun: You may outnumber us. You may outthink us. / But hear this, you of the West — / you will never be crazier than we are…!
Every Goguryeo wall prays to the Holy King. Who was he? We go back seven hundred years, to the day the sun stopped…!

=== EPISODE 37: Haemosu (-37) [flashback]
The sky is empty first. Then come five dragons in the yoke, gold, crimson, azure, jade and white, and behind them a small gold chariot cutting the noon on the run they make every day. From the ground it is a fleck and a wheel, nothing a bather could call a face. The driver stands in it the way a man stands in a doorway he owns, one palm on the rail, laughing at nothing in particular.
Dawn, noon, dusk, night, always the same route. Below, the Amnok is a line he is not supposed to break: wet stone, morning shallows with no boat in them, rocks that are only rocks.
Haemosu, god of the sun, has kept this hour since before the river had daughters. Today the Amnok flashes under the wheel. He looks down, and the hour breaks.
In the shallows, three river-daughters are bathing: Yuhwa and her two sisters. Wet hair down their backs, the river at their hips. Nobody dressed for heaven. He falls in love and in lust in the same glance.
Hwahye and Wihye have left their silk on the rocks. The eldest folded hers once; the middle did not bother. Yuhwa’s ice-blue is still on her shoulder, wet.
Yuhwa kneels in the shallows with her hair in one fist like a dark rope and rinses the river out of it without hurrying. Heaven can wait on a rinse; she has decided that without saying it. With her back to the sky she looks over her shoulder, as if someone up there had said her name.
haemosu: …Stop. Stop the chariot.
haemosu: Those thighs… / The water…
yuhwa: Unni. / Go. I’m here. / …I was going to say don’t look up.
hwahye: Hey. In. / Now. You hear me?
Hwahye dives first and does not look back. The eldest treats the sky like a timetable she will not miss.
wihye: Pfft— wait up. / You, seriously— / Whatever, I’m going—
Wihye laughs and follows, a splash that is mostly amusement.
Two wakes cut the shallows and close. Yuhwa stays. She gets up off her knees, looks straight up as if she had been waiting for heaven to notice, and draws her wet hair over one shoulder.
She draws the wet silk higher, one hip and then the other, and lets the sun finish looking.
haemosu: Hey— / Wait. Hey. You. / Why aren’t you hiding? Look at me like that and I’m coming down.
yuhwa: Heaven looks down every day. / So today I’m supposed to blush? / …Come closer, if you want to see. / Into the water. / And decide… where your hands are going.
haemosu: …Your name. / I need it… before I come down. / Or… I kiss you without one.
yuhwa: Come down first. / From the sky it’s an order. / At the water… I’ll hear it as a request. / Ask with your mouth… and I’ll answer with my name.
He forgets how to swallow, a god doing a mortal’s small panic. Then he grins, and the grin arrives before the plan. He leaves the rail and the hour in the same motion, the dragons keep the joke going without him, and the water takes him at the knee.
He wades close. She does not run. He stops where a stranger should stop. Then he doesn’t.
haemosu: Why didn’t you run away? / Your sisters did.
yuhwa: …Didn’t see any reason. / The water’s cold. You’re warm. That’s all there is to it.
haemosu: Look straight at the sun / and you burn.
yuhwa: Oh, is that so? / Then I should blink.
haemosu: It’ll burn your eyes out. / I’m not a lamp.
yuhwa: I like what I see. / I’m looking anyway. You came down. / Don’t make me say it twice.
He swallows. The grin survives it. Barely.
She tips her mouth and asks whether the sun likes what it sees, silk already losing the argument with the water.
yuhwa: This way. The bank. / The sky has too many sisters.
He follows like the hour had been her idea.
The copper room rises on the bank like a kiln. He builds it the same afternoon, because the open sky has become too many witnesses.
yuhwa: Copper gets hot in summer. / …You’ll know if you touch it. / My back, too. / If you press me to it… you won’t tell which burned you.
haemosu: I know. / That’s why I can’t take my hands off you. / Or my mouth.
yuhwa: Then don’t. / Not while heaven is watching.
yuhwa: And while it watches… deeper.
She kisses him with river still on her mouth. The kiss tastes like the shallows. He makes a sound he will deny.
Inside, the copper has kept the afternoon’s heat. She leans into it and does not look away from him. Gold lies across wet skin in a hard bar, and the ice-blue silk slips from one shoulder, then gives up the other.
yuhwa: If you want it, say so. / I’m not asking twice.
yuhwa: Give me— all of it. / Don’t save any.
The copper is already hot. He puts her back to it anyway. The river-silk is gathered at her hip and her thighs close around a sun-god who has never learned to be gentle with an hour. She takes him in with the same wet hand that washed her hair for heaven, and when he is all the way inside her she laughs, as if this were what she had meant by looking.
yuhwa: Haa— is heaven always this heavy? / More— against the copper— don’t stop—
haemosu: I broke the hour. / I don’t care. / Your name— now—
yuhwa: Yuhwa— ah— it’s Yuhwa— / Stay— stay inside me— / All of it— the whole sun—
He takes her through the heat of the wall, gold on wet skin, and every stroke knocks a sound out of her that the river throws back. She comes first and loudly, looking up as if heaven were still watching. Then he spills into her, a god’s whole careless heat, and does not draw back, because she told him not to, and because the hour is already ruined.
The copper keeps the afternoon. Outside, the river goes on being a river.
## Habek's Court
The copper is still warm when the river notices. The Amnok keeps its own court: Habek, god of the river and father of three daughters, stands on the wet stones as if the current were a hall. Mist is the dais. He does not need a chair.
habek: Who stopped the chariot. Say a name.
yuhwa: I… looked up. / I just— looked. That’s all it was.
habek: You don’t sleep in my mist after that. / You smell like copper.
habek: Go. The bank is closed.
Hwahye and Wihye do not argue the sentence. The eldest watches the current. The middle one watches the copper glow die. Neither looks at their father’s face.
Habek kicks Yuhwa out with a look, not a foot. The bank understands.
The pavilion walkway does not catch her. Habek’s sleeve is already the closed door. She hits packed earth with ice-blue still wet from the copper.
For a while nobody comes. The mist that used to be a bed is just weather. She sits where the river can see her and does not look up.
The sky talks first. She hears him before she sees anything with paws.
haemosu: Hey. / Wait. Don’t sit in the dust. / Follow the fox.
The fox is already on the packed earth, pale gold-white, looking back once as if she might miss the joke. Yuhwa follows it south, barefoot, the ice-blue gone dull with dust: pine shade, a river-bend that is not the Amnok, a pass of bare stone where she is smaller than the ridge. The fox does not explain the map.
From the river, Buyeo’s capital is a palisade of timber teeth and a hill of grey roofs. The studded doors open. King Geumwa, the gold-frog king, comes out to the yard himself.
geumwa: Come in. I’ve got a room free. / The yard can learn your name later.
A sun-shaft finds her where she kneels to wring the river out of her sleeve. When she crosses the yard at night it moves with her, a bar of gold keeping her sleeve.
Yuhwa’s ice-blue sleeve is the first roof the boy will remember, though he is not a boy yet.
In time Yuhwa lays a great egg. Geumwa has the egg taken from her before the court has agreed what a river-daughter is allowed to bear.
Dogs won't eat it. An axe won't split it. What on earth is inside Yuhwa's egg…?

=== EPISODE 38: Buyeo (-37) [flashback]
## The Egg
Dogs and pigs will not eat it; the sty refuses the guest, and the ministers pretend that is a kind of answer. In the road, cattle and horses step around it, hooves knowing better than the hall. In the open field, birds cover it with their wings instead of pecking, and the yard goes quiet at that.
An axe is brought. The axe will not split the egg. The edge sings and the shell does not bother to crack.
Someone winds up with both arms and hurls it off the palisade. It meets the stones and stays whole.
Yuhwa wraps it warm in her own sleeve and takes it back upstairs, and nobody reaches for the axe again.
Then the shell gives, and out comes a baby boy, wet and furious, already trying to focus. He looks up as if the room had owed him an explanation.
They name him Jumong, the good shot, because in those days people were named for what heaven had plainly already decided. He grows up with his brothers Daeso and Galsa, and the better he shoots, the smaller their smiles become.
They are boys first, three princes at one stake in one square, before anybody is an heir on purpose. They shoot with borrowed bows, too long in the arm.
Jumong can find a fly’s wing with an arrow before the bow fits his arm.
jumong: I’ll take the fly.
Daeso teaches the grip, then resents the hit. The lesson ends the moment the arrow is better than the teacher.
The yard hears the wood take it, a clean tick, and the praise does not arrive. Daeso keeps his hands on his own bow as if applause were a confession. Galsa looks at the dirt instead of the hit.
They sleep in a pile like dogs under one quilt, and in the morning the quilt has taken sides. Jumong steals the last millet and grins through it, which is worse than the theft.
Yuhwa watches from the hall door, ice-blue sleeve on the post, not stepping into the boys’ weather.
They grow apart in the same square, a hand’s width more between bowls each season.
Only two come back talking from the stake. The third has already started a country in his head.
Grown, they still shoot at the princes’ mark-stake. Daeso stands too close when Jumong’s arrow lands.
daeso: Do not outshoot the house that feeds you.
jumong: Then put the mark farther.
galsa: If it lands, I meant to applaud.
Jumong keeps the grin because grinning is cheaper than asking why, and Daeso hates the price.
Galsa will not stay to be the second smile in that hall. East of Buyeo he splits a smaller country and names it for himself — Galsa-Buyeo.
Jumong’s arranged marriage to Lady Ye is a hall’s solution: a wife, a lamp, a door that still opens onto Buyeo.
Lady Ye gets pregnant with their son Yuri while the yard is still pretending the foundling is a guest.
Geumwa will not take the heir’s counsel, so Daeso takes the ministers into a side room. Lamp low. If they write it down, the scandal arrives before the knife.
daeso: Do it before the next hunt. / Quiet is fine.
Geumwa answers his heir the way tired kings answer. He refuses the knife and gives the foundling a chore instead: Jumong is sent to the royal stables, which in Buyeo is where a hall keeps a prince it would rather not see at dinner.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 13, Goguryeo Annals — Jumong; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1] The king did not listen, and set him to tending the horses. Jumong knew which ones were swift; he cut their feed and made them lean, and fed the sluggish ones well and made them fat. The king rode the fat ones himself and gave the lean one to Jumong.
Yuhwa comes to the stable after the lamps are out, a river-daughter in a frog-king’s straw, and finds her son brushing the best horse in Buyeo as if he could apologise to it in advance.
yuhwa: This one, isn’t it? / The fast one.
jumong: …How’d you know? / I didn’t tell anyone.
yuhwa: You brush this one longer than the others. / I’ll give you a needle. Put it in his tongue. / Say sorry later, and feed him till he bursts.
jumong: Mother, you’re terrifying. / …For how many days?
yuhwa: Until Daeso’s done sharpening.
By the next moon the fastest horse in the yard looks like a rack of kindling with a mane, and the slow ones shine like lacquer. Geumwa walks the stalls, picks the fattest for himself, and tosses the thin one to the foundling with a joke about how well they match. Daeso laughs loudest, which is a pity, because he is the one man in Buyeo who should have looked twice.
geumwa: Suits you. / You both eat my rice and still stay thin.
jumong: Thank you, Majesty. / I’ll take good care of him.
He pulls the needle out that night. The horse eats until dawn.
Before the next hunt, a knife finds Jumong in the dark and misses.
ladyye: Leave Buyeo. Tonight. / I’ll keep the lamp.
jumong: Leave the door half open. / So I know which way is still yours.
Night at the palisade. Iron studs, a red sleeve, and a wife who does not come out to wave.
His friends Oi, Mari and Hyupbo take the hills with him. Behind them come the riders Daeso sent, less a hunt than a net, and under the pines it closes from above.
## The Flight
They split in the pines before the river, four men and one horse between them, the one Geumwa thought was thin.
oi: We’ll take the ridge. / Find us when you still have a bow.
jumong: Take him. / Your road over the ridge is longer. I’ll do the river alone.
oi: Are you crazy? He’s your horse.
jumong: Exactly. Fatten him up for me. / …I’ll come find you.
He runs until the pines smear. Behind him the net is spears in the dark, points only, no faces he is allowed to know.
Something keeps pace with him above the trees, black on black, going from branch to branch without seeming to hurry. A crow. He is too frightened to count its legs.
Jumong reaches the water alone, his death already written down for that day. No ford. No boat. The friends are a ridge away, on purpose.
Haewonmek, the reaper who collects each day’s dead, is already in the air. He skims the river toward him. Black hat, black silk, mouth bound shut. Jumong doesn’t see him. He’s looking at the water and the rain.
A root takes his foot. He goes down on the wet stones, pine needles in his mouth, the bow a pace off as if it had been the first thing taken. Haewonmek crouches over him to collect what is owed, and the blow is already coming down.
The cloak arrives before the face. Rain fills it. A hand closes on Haewonmek’s wrist from behind, and the strike simply stops — the way an elder stops a sleeve that has gone too far.
Jumong’s cheek is in the mud. Haewonmek looks back. Behind him, in a dark hood, the sun god is holding his wrist and laughing, as if the night had grabbed the wrong man. The night is Haewonmek’s road. The joke is Haemosu’s.
haewonmek: Haemosu… / The night is not your domain…!
haemosu: Heh… / Do you really think the sun disappears at night? / I was just crossing the ocean when I heard you coming over.
haewonmek: This man is fated to die today… / You are not to interfere with Yumla’s domain…!
haemosu: Hey, Haewonmek. / I’ll leave my little brother alone while he’s at his new job. / But this is my son. / And he still hasn’t completed his purpose in this world. / And besides… I outrank you. / If Yumla has any complaints, tell him to come see me himself.
He puts Haewonmek aside and leans to Jumong’s ear. Jumong cannot see him, only the night, the river, a warmth that should not be there. The idea arrives as breath.
## The Crossing
jumong: I am the son of the great Haemosu, the lord of the sun! / Make way for me!
The river answers. Tortoises rise and lock shell to shell in the dark. Jumong runs the wet backs as if they had always been a road.
The two brothers stay on the near stones. Jumong is already a red speck on the far dark. Haemosu throws an arm across Haewonmek’s shoulder and laughs like the job is done. Haewonmek’s gat is still askew — the look of a clerk whose ledger just walked off.
haewonmek: He is still mortal…
haemosu: Yes, of course. / But you know… every man comes into this world for a purpose. / He’s going to do great things. / When his time comes, I’ll let you take him.
haemosu: Look at him go. / That's my boy.
haewonmek: You just robbed a ledger.
haemosu: I borrowed a day. / I'll give it back.
haewonmek: Yumla isn’t going to like this…
The bird that watches him is not an ordinary crow. On Goguryeo’s banners it will stand on three legs under a red sun, the samjoko, the bird that can look at the day without blinking.
It is sitting on a rock on the far bank when he comes off the last shell, soaked, laughing like an idiot because he is alive. This time he counts.
jumong: …One, two. / Three? / Hey. Why’ve you got three legs?
The crow looks at him without blinking, which is either rude or holy, then drops off the rock, flies ten paces into the pines, lands again, and looks back.
jumong: Follow you? / …If you’re leading me to a bear, I swear I’m roasting you. / Three legs. There’d be one to spare.
He follows it all afternoon, uphill, through pines that stop being Buyeo’s and start being nobody’s. It keeps ten paces ahead and never once lets him catch up. At dusk it lands on a stone lip above a dark opening in the hill and stays there, folded, like a doorman whose shift is over.
jumong: …Here? / Thanks. Really. / Can’t roast you now, can I.
Before the valley has a name for him he goes in, into stone and leaf-light and a country-shaped dark. In what will be called the Jumong cavern, he prays for a roof of his own.
A soaked exile, a hall full of spears, and a chieftain's daughter who won't look at him. Jumong's luck is about to get complicated…!

=== EPISODE 39: Jolbon (-37) [flashback]
## The Scouts
He is still wet from the river when the pines stop being empty. Two men in Yeon leather, spears too casual to be hunting, too careful to be lost. Jolbon scouts find him first. The bow is already in the pine needles. His hands are empty and shaking anyway.
Scout: Stop— stop stop— / Bow—
Second scout: I got him I got— / Red. That’s not ours.
jumong: Down. It’s down. / Don’t— spear. Please. / Water—
Scout: Hands. Hands where I can see. / You deaf?
jumong: Yeah. Yeah look. / Just— I ran. River. That’s it.
Second scout: Name. Fast. / If Tabal has to come out here I’m blaming you.
jumong: Jumong. / Jumong. That’s— that’s the name.
Scout: You’ll get Tabal. / Walk. If you trip I swear—
He looks past the spear. The pine behind the man is a better door than the man’s face.
They bring him in at dusk, not as a guest. One scout keeps looking back like the pines might grow more men. The valley opens under grey giwa. On the porch Yeon Tabal, chieftain of Jolbon, holds a cup he is not drinking.
## Tabal’s Hall
Tabal walks him across the packed earth like a man showing a storeroom to a thief: grain porch, well, pine, five roofs that will not share a yard.
Inside, the hall is torches and a man who has not offered a mat. They put Jumong on his knees, packed earth in the weave of his red silk. He tries a grin. It does not survive the torches.
yeontabal: So who sent you.
jumong: Nobody sent me. / Your men grabbed me. I was just— here.
yeontabal: I asked for a name.
jumong: Jumong. / That’s the name.
yeontabal: Your clothes don’t look like anything nearby. / Mohe? Khitan? Or the commandery?
At Tabal’s shoulder stands a woman in dusty-rose silk with a tally-stick in her hand. She has not looked at him once.
jumong: Pretty. Just—
yeontabal: Eyes. Front.
sosuno: Count the dirt. / Not him.
jumong: Ow— I said it.
He thinks it with his mouth shut: So this is how I die, for a compliment, in a hall that smells like pine smoke.
Tabal notices the bow. The wood is wrong for every hand in the room except one.
They put Jumong’s bow in Tabal’s hands. He cannot pull the string, and the limb does not do him the courtesy of bending.
yeontabal: Stop! / Hands off him. / …Whose son are you.
jumong: Son of Haemosu. / The bow knows. I didn’t ask it to.
He gives it back, and the wood stays as it was, which is worse than if it had snapped.
yeontabal: You're a slave. My daughter's. / Shed. You hunt, you eat. / I do not want ash tracked into my hall.
For a week Tabal uses him like a tool he has not paid for. West millet has a boar. Two cousins have a ditch and a knife each. Jumong hits both problems and sits in the dirt until someone tells him to stand. Tabal does not thank him. He just stops inventing work.
yeontabal: The millet likes you. I don’t. / Stay anyway. / Shed stays the shed.
jumong: Yes sir. / …The well’s nicer though.
yeontabal: Then go fetch. Out.
## The Hunt Muster
Tabal’s daughter Sosuno, a widow, is already on the grain porch, running Jolbon before she has priced the exile: spear-count, west line, who eats, who rides. The yard answers her first and her father second.
sosuno: West line. Two short. / You. Spear. Not that one, the one that isn’t bent. / We leave at first light. If you’re late I leave you.
A hunter: Yes—
sosuno: Not yes. The count. / East, you’re overlapping. Split. / If I have to say it twice you sit the hunt out.
A hunter: —Split. Sorry.
She does not smile when they move. She does not thank them. She does not raise her voice. The spears go where the chin points.
Then the wet man is in the yard. Red silk. A back she has not counted. The yard goes quiet. Nobody dropped a spear. They just stopped being loud, because she did.
Something in her goes stupid while the chin stays up. His father’s name she heard in the hall and filed under nonsense. The line of a shoulder she cannot file anywhere. She will deny all of this to the millet.
sosuno: …Next. / I said next. / Don’t look at me. Look at the line.
Little Sosuno is purring so loud she can hear it in her teeth. Hungry. Stupid. Staring at his mouth like it is a job. She keeps the spear-count going with a voice that does not shake. The other voice is not for the yard.
sosuno: Oh you like him. You like him immediately. Shut up. / Look at that face. That chest. Wet. I could— / Not here. Not with father. Purr quieter. I said quieter—
yeontabal: Sosuno. / The line.
sosuno: I have the line. / West is short two. I said that. / Sun’s in my eyes.
Chin up, she is her father’s hall. Then his red back crosses the packed earth and the chin fails when nobody is looking. Heat at the throat.
The counting-voice says one, two, three. The other voice puts his mouth at her neck. Outside, she is already walking away.
She starts calling him names because looking is worse. Big idiot is the one that sticks. He answers to it on the third day, cheerful, which makes it worse.
She points him at the west millet with two fingers, the way she points at weather, and he hauls the sacks grinning as if the job were a favor. The porch hears the laugh and pretends it is a cough.
sosuno: Wrong stack. Do it again. / Ditch. Now. And don’t talk in the ditch. / Count the sacks. Don’t grin.
She makes him wring the rope until his hands complain, and she watches the hands, not the grin.
sosuno: Pull. Don’t chat with the rope. / Grinning’s extra. I didn’t order it.
She tells the yard, and herself, Work first. Looking later. The yard believes her. She doesn’t.
Soon the porch has a name for him too: Sosuno’s worker. She hates how easily it fits.
sosuno: It's not like that. Worker. / Move the sack.
sosuno: That’s my worker. / Not yours to stare at.
jumong: So how long has it been.
sosuno: Don’t— don’t grin like you found something.
jumong: Then why are you furiously blushing.
sosuno: I’m also not stopping. / The count. Not you.
sosuno: Move.
jumong: Hi.
sosuno: Not hi. / Around. Big idiot. / Don’t follow me.
jumong: Wasn’t. / Well’s that way.
sosuno: Other water exists. / Use it.
jumong: Moving. / See? Moved. / You’re fun when you’re like this.
sosuno: I’m not fun. / I’m working. / Don’t grin at the work.
One morning she dumps a bucket at his boots and does not bother pretending it slipped. He laughs. Then he says it like it is nothing.
sosuno: Watch it. / Or don’t. Drown. Whatever.
jumong: Hey. / You’re pretty when you’re mean. / Like— actually. Sorry. Not sorry.
sosuno: Ha—!? / Who’s— pretty, what— / It’s not like that!! / Big idiot. Go. Go go—
jumong: Going. Going. / Sleeve’s wet. Thanks.
He wrings the sleeve on the way to the shed. She waits until the yard is empty. Then she hides her whole face in the dusty-rose, red to the hairline, whispering idiot at nobody.
## Upstairs
She does not stay in the yard. Chin still up, she takes the loft stairs two at a time like a woman with grain to count. The window faces the millet: his shirt off, red silk knotted at the hip, a back doing work. Whose son he is can wait. The muscles cannot.
Sosuno lies on her thatched bed the first night and tells the thatch she is only tired.
She tries to fight it with a count. The count knows his mouth.
His face comes first, then the rest of him, arriving in the dark behind her eyes; she gets stuck on the bare back the yard already ruined her with. Her hand slips down between her legs while the other stays over her mouth, as if the mouth were the scandal. She imagines him inside her and hates the thought even as she spends it, then scolds the heat for using his face. The heat does not apologize.
The first night does not leave the bed. Morning will have to come up the stairs and fetch her.
Another afternoon. The dusty-rose is hiked, her thighs apart on the timber, one hand over her mouth and the other talking to the part of her that does not run a hunt: Little Sosuno.
sosuno: Idiot. Don’t grin in my head. / This is your fault, big idiot.
sosuno: Little Sosuno… you’re hungry today aren’t you… / I don’t blame you…. mmm! look at him… / Those big muscles…. chest…. back…. / Ah fuck dripping wet again… / Out hunting for meat… / I want you to fill me up with some of that meat….
Tabal is in the doorway of the yard, not the loft, and his voice still climbs the stairs.
yeontabal: Sosuno! / West count. Now. / Don’t make me climb.
She freezes mid-breath. She smooths the dusty-rose, wipes her hands on her sleeve, and takes the stairs with her chin up. By the packed earth she is the chieftain’s eldest again.
sosuno: West is short two. / I counted. Twice. / Don’t send the exile. He’ll get lost.
yeontabal: He hit the boar. / You just don’t like his back.
sosuno: I don’t like his anything. / Can we do the millet.
## Other Daughters
Word gets out that the exile hits what he aims at and looks like a sun when he works shirtless. Jolbon women find reasons to fetch water. Other chieftains mention daughters. Sosuno is suddenly everywhere those reasons are. She finds a flaw every time.
A chieftain: My girl can count. / Strong arms. Good hall.
sosuno: He walks into buckets. / Can’t wring a sleeve. Talks to millet. / You’d be bored in a week. Big idiot. Next.
He flirts at the wrong well, which is any well she can see from the porch, and the girls laugh too long at a sentence he did not finish.
Teal: Hey big boy~
jumong: You’re— yeah. Funny. Too funny.
Teal: Don’t look at Sosuno. Look at me.
Teal: Don’t follow me. / Unless you are.
Teal hikes her hem at his well like a dare, the rope between them a bad idea, and leans hip first on the beam. The timber takes her weight. His ears take the rest.
Plum: Come fetch at ours.
Plum does not bother with the beam. She turns and backs into him, a joke with a body, laughing as if the bucket had asked, then does it again, meaner and prettier, waiting for the porch to break.
A Sosuno-shaped shadow falls across the rim before her voice does. She is holding an empty bucket she does not need. The girls notice the shadow first, and the laugh dies.
Jumong’s grin dies in his mouth when he sees who is holding the empty bucket.
They can do sexy. She can do eldest, which is a worse weapon, and she knows it before they do.
sosuno: Get. Off. / Get off my well.
sosuno: This well’s ours. / Ditch is that way. / He doesn’t need help. He needs to work.
A girl: We were only—
sosuno: You. Bucket. / That well is not a porch. / Go home before I tell your mother you can’t count steam.
jumong: I was just—
sosuno: You. Shed. / Don’t smile at them. / Don’t smile at me either.
He waits until the girls are gone. Then he does not go to the shed. He follows her to the grain post and says it like weather.
jumong: So. / You keep chasing them off.
sosuno: BECAUSE YOU WERE HANGING WITH THOSE OTHER BITCHES—
jumong: The well girls. That chieftain’s kid. You told her I talk to millet.
sosuno: BECAUSE YOU DO— / WHO ASKED YOU— / I don’t— they’re in the WAY— / This is MY yard— MY well—
jumong: Okay. Okay. / You’re screaming. / I’m just asking why I can’t say hi.
sosuno: DON’T HI THEM. / DON’T HI ME. / BIG IDIOT. GET— get off my post—
She is screaming mad and pink to the hairline and everyone on the porch can hear the hide crack. He grins. That is worse. She leaves him the post. The well she keeps for tomorrow.
## The Well
Day at the well is two buckets and a rope that already knows her hands.
They keep meeting there as if the rim were a coincidence.
jumong: Rope’s being a villain. / Want me to—
sosuno: Pull or don’t. / Talking doesn’t fill it. / Don’t look at my face. / …Sosuno. / There. Now pull.
jumong: Sosuno. / Cute name. / Your ears are pink.
sosuno: Wind. / Don’t— look. / You’re so dumb. Pull.
jumong: There’s no wind. / You waited, huh.
sosuno: I was here first. / That’s water. / If you mhm I will kill you. / Pull.
He keeps ending up thirsty at the same hour. She keeps being there. On the fourth morning he stops pretending the rope is the problem and kisses her at the well-beam.
She does not pull away first. When she turns, the dusty-rose is wet at the waist from the rope, and she looks back over her shoulder.
sosuno: You— / How dare you. / My father’s well— / I will kill you. / After. Move.
jumong: You kissed back. / Just saying.
sosuno: Did not. / Surprise. / The second bucket isn’t full. / That’s all I said.
jumong: Okay. / Waiting. / You’re kinda sexy when you threaten me. / I’ll shut up. I’ll shut up.
sosuno: Ha!? Stop it— that’s embarrassing— / It’s not like that!! / Draw. Go. Go—
He takes the full bucket and actually goes. She stands at the rim until he is a red speck at the shed. Then both hands over her face, furious, shaking.
She has been collecting him: a thread, a fletch, a length of well-rope, a scrap of his headband, folded into a cloth behind the grain-porch post. He finds it. He holds it up.
jumong: Hey. / Mice don’t fold headbands. / You hide these like a thief.
She goes so red the dusty-rose looks pale. She snatches and misses.
sosuno: Those are— inventory. / Trash. I’ll burn them. / Don’t grin. If you grin I— give it—
jumong: You’re beautiful when you lie. / Want it back so you can steal it again?
sosuno: Pretty, my foot— ha— / Shut up. Big idiot. / That’s not— funny—
He stops smiling. Not angry. Done. He unslings the bow and lays it on packed earth at the well-rim. Then he walks.
jumong: Keep it. / I’m gonna go. / Tell the millet thanks.
She does not call stay. She picks the bow up too fast. One arrow. The timber well-beam beside his ear takes it. He stops.
sosuno: Wait— wait wait— / Don’t. Don’t turn around. / If you look I can’t—
The confession comes like a tooth she has been biting since the porch. She talks to the dirt, the bow, anything but his mouth.
The bird pin comes out in her own fingers. Her hair falls in a sheet and the well-rim disappears behind it. She sits on the packed earth with the dusty-rose in a heap and the bow beside her knee, forehead toward the boards of the well, close enough to smell wet stone, and keeps talking into the dirt because his face is a luxury she has not paid for.
He kneels lower than her crown, careful of the hair.
sosuno: I don’t— I don’t like you.
jumong: Then I’m going.
Then he grins, smaller than the yard grin, asking.
sosuno: I wasn’t going to say it. / I was gonna let you leave. Stupid. Fine. / Then you put the bow down and I— / I want you. There. Stay. / Don’t make me— I can’t twice. / Big idiot. Other ear. I swear.
Sosuno hears herself and cannot take it back. The dirt has heard it now. So has he.
jumong: Hey. Hey I’m here. / Look. Still here. / Come here. You’re shaking.
They do not make it to a feast. The grain-room lamp is closer than pride.
jumong: Hey. / Numbers later. / Your throat’s brighter than the lamp. Sorry. Not sorry.
sosuno: I am not your wife yet. / Don’t— my hands. / Counting hand or me. / …Big idiot. / It’s not like that.
jumong: Only you. / From the first look. / Give me your mouth… first. / Country later.
sosuno: Then take it. / Don’t put a price on it. / I already lost the count.
sosuno: Now come here before I take it back.
She hits his chest, once, not hard enough. Then she is on his mouth like she is angry at it.
The dusty-rose hiked, she braces against the sacks with her back to him, pulls him in by the collar and tells him she hates him in the same breath. Then she feels the weight of him, and the hate gets specific. Love and spite in one grip.
sosuno: It won’t— ah— fit—
She does not stop, furious at the fit and more furious at the thought of stopping.
sosuno: Look at my back.
jumong: Hate me then. / Harder. / God you’re— look at you.
sosuno: Look— look at you— that chest— that back— those hips I watched from the loft— / That sound. Wet. Slap. That’s— that’s Little Sosuno, she’s— ah— dripping, she— / Take it. That sexy— man meat— I said take it and— destroy my tight little ass— / Beat her up. Beat up Little Sosuno till she’s just wet. Nothing left. That’s all she is—
jumong: Hey. Hey— / Or don’t. God. / Look at you talking.
sosuno: Don’t slow. Don’t be nice. I said destroy— / I want the slap. The noise when you— when you hit that wet— again— again— / Fill her. Ruin her. She’s been hungry since the yard went quiet— / Well girls don’t get this. Mine. Little Sosuno is mine to— ah— wreck—
jumong: Little Sosuno. / Cute. / I’ve got both of you.
sosuno: Don’t NAME her don’t— ah— she can hear— she likes it she likes it— / Deeper. The meat. All of it. Don’t you dare pull out— / AHH— DON’T STOP— / DUMB BIG IDIOT—
jumong: That’s it— / I’ve got you. / Take it—
He spends himself in her against the grain sacks, and she bites his shoulder so she will not have to hear herself. It does not help. The loft-voice is still in the room.
sosuno: I didn’t— you didn’t hear destroy— I don’t talk like— / Little Sosuno isn’t— I don’t have a— / Forget it. Get out. Don’t look at me.
jumong: I heard. / You can talk like that. / It’s you. It’s hot. I’m keeping you. Both.
Later the lamp has burned down to a bead, and he is still holding on to her as if she were something that might spill.
sosuno: Don’t— don’t be nice. / I’ll get stupid. / I am not— melting. I’m a chieftain’s daughter. I’m not— shy. / …Stay. Not because you asked.
jumong: Hey. / You’re beautiful. / Water. You want?
sosuno: Get— no. Door. Close it if you go. / Don’t look at my back.
He goes for water. The door shuts. She lasts three breaths. Then she slides down the sacks with both palms over her mouth, scarlet, furious at a word he already left. Beautiful.
Little Sosuno.
She mouths idiot at the timber until it is safe to stand.
Tabal has been on the porch since before the arrow. Morning makes it public.
yeontabal: The pine. / Hundred paces. Now. / Hit, he eats. Miss, I throw him. / I am not pleased. I am also not blind.
The pine stands a hundred paces off across packed earth. Sosuno grips the porch rail, knuckles white, chin up.
He turns for the pine with the easy shoulder of a man who already knows the knot.
The best men hit bark. Tabal hits the knot. Jumong splits Tabal’s arrow down the shaft, and the hall hears the wood cry.
jumong: …Yeah. / Still here.
Silence. Then Tabal laughs — short, unwilling. Sosuno’s hand is already on the rail.
yeontabal: Eat. / Road can wait. / My daughter—
sosuno: The bow is the bow. / Don’t. / I only— lost the count. / Big idiot. Stop smiling.
yeontabal: Ha. / River was supposed to take him. Daughter ran after it. / Sosuno. You picked. You keep. No feast. / Jumong. Hurt her, bow won’t save you. / Eat. Stay. Grumble like the rest of us.
Tabal sets a vermilion cord where a feast would have been, a short red line, two people who have already spent the night.
## Five Tribes
Jolbon is five roofs that will not share a yard. Cousins cut cousins over a ditch, a ford, a winter store. Jumong watches it for a week and then says it in the hall, easy, the way he hauls sacks.
jumong: You keep cutting each other. / A ditch is not a country. / I crossed a river on turtles. You fight over who owns the mud.
yeontabal: …Watch your mouth. / Those are my cousins. / They have been mine longer than you have been dry.
jumong: Then make them one hall. / Five fires, one roof. / Or keep the ditches. I can leave a bow on dirt again.
He does not conquer them. He walks the five yards with the same grin he used on Sosuno, and the same refusal to be impressed by a feud. Grain is counted in one book. Fords are shared. A cousin who draws in the ditch finds Jumong already there, bow unstrung, talking about weather until the cousin looks stupid.
What he calls a talk, the valley will call the first summit of the five tribes: five fires in a ring the yard can hold, no dais, knees, a ditch demoted to a line on the ground. For once the smoke agrees.
## The First King
After the marriage the five tribes sit in Tabal’s hall and do the thing they hate more than a ditch: they agree. They vote Jumong first king. Nobody remembers him asking; the grin had already become a roof.
The Crow roof votes with the others, a dark sleeve, a short nod, the king already grinning like it hurts.
yeontabal: …Fine. / King, then. / If the ditches start again I will say I told you. / Eat. Stay. Wear it.
jumong: I will. / Not for the chair. / For the roof.
Sosuno is the first queen of a country that still smells like millet. The cord is still new. The sacks have not learned to be tribute.
King and queen on packed earth, no throne between them, the yard they already know how to fight in.
He sleeps beside a queen who still counts fires, one, two, three, even with a crown in the room.
In the new room the dusty-rose has gone richer; the dare is the same. She turns him over and looks at the back she once inventoried from a porch.
sosuno: Like a queen, then. / Don’t you dare be gentle about the title.
The blushing queen still hides her mouth in her own wrist.
sosuno: I’m blushing— don’t you dare stop
## The Pine Kingdom
Word reaches the millet porch: Oi, Mari, and Hyupbo did not vanish. They reached a pine roof that is not Tabal’s.
It is the Pine Kingdom, a stand of old pines with a hall under them, where Song Yang, king of the pine roof, has been feeding them and deciding what they are worth. Jumong goes to fetch them himself.
songyang: This pine country had a name before you hatched.
jumong: Then put the name on the mark. / One arrow. Then we talk.
Song Yang’s arrow is honest and short. It hits wood. It does not hit the knot.
songyang: The pine country is under this roof. / Take the three. They ate.
At dusk the three come out of the pine hall, earth-tone silk, thinner, grinning like men who were not sure of the door.
Years later, the bow will wait on packed earth, and the yard will be quieter than a feast, which is how this country keeps a death.
## Dawn in the Cavern
Later he goes back to the mouth in the hill, the same stone and the same leaf-light, to pray the way a man prays when a hall has already named him and he still does not quite believe the name. Night thins. At dawn the light breaks through.
jumong: Father! / If you’re listening— they made me king. Me. Of a whole valley. What am I supposed to do with it?
Gold where the dark had been, and too tall for a lamp. Haemosu lets himself be seen at last: silver-white hair, the sun’s hour delayed on purpose, looking at his son the way he once looked down from a chariot rail.
haemosu: Jumong…. my son…
jumong: Father… are you even listening to me?
haemosu: It is to build a new world. / Build a world of your own…. my son…!
He comes out of the cavern a king the valley already voted for, and a son who finally saw the face that had been the hour. The chronicles start the years from here. His descendants will push the borders until Goryeo is the largest kingdom in Samhan — a later argument, a later map. This morning is only a roof, a grin, and a gold break in the stone.
## Two Sons
Sosuno’s boys, Onjo and Biryu, watch the well the way other boys watch a hunt. Rope, bucket, their mother’s chin.
onjo: Mother’s counting again. / I’m staying near the porch.
biryu: I’m going farther. When I’m bigger. / Don’t tell her I said that.
## Dongmyung
sosuno: You learn something from founding a country twice. / The second one is easier.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 13, Goguryeo Annals — Jumong; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 218 · cf. Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonder 1 — Old Buyeo / Jumong] I am the son of the Heavenly Emperor, grandson of the River Earl. Today I flee, and those who pursue me have nearly arrived — what shall I do? Thereupon the fish and turtles formed a bridge.
[FLASHBACK -24 Buyeo, five winters before]
  Word comes from Buyeo while the new country is still learning its name. Yuhwa has stopped. The hall that took her in keeps the body. The door that opens next is not a mortal door.
  Heat in a room that had gone cold. Gold where the lamp had failed. Haemosu is simply there — chariot left in the yard like a horse someone could not bear to stable.
  haemosu: Yuhwa. / I didn’t give this to my little brother. / Your hand.
  yuhwa: You’re late. / The copper room… stayed warm. Even when you weren’t in it.
  haemosu: That time I came down. / This time you come up. / There’s an empty seat. On the side where I set.
  yuhwa: That light… it isn’t the one I looked up at from the shallows. / It’s cold. / Still… across from you is fine.
  haemosu: Then come. / The chariot yields the night.
  He does not ask a question. She takes the hand that once could not let go of her. Buyeo keeps a grave. Its records say a river-daughter died. The sky, which keeps poorer records, has a moon the next night.
Jumong spends the rest of his life driving the western commanderies from the river valleys, and the country grows the way countries grow in old stories: one bowshot, one bride, one sworn brother at a time. He dies in the autumn of the year Yuri comes south. The hall names him Dongmyung, Bright of the East, and leaves his bow on the packed earth.
The chronicles will not write that the Yeon hall never forgot weighing a Go exile. Centuries later another Yeon will speak in the same short heat — and call the country by its longest name, as if shortening it were already kneeling to a softer king.
Back in Surabol, the queen is failing and the council must name who's next. It only takes one hand to lock the door…!
